rationale: A wins because it keeps the founder out of invented-story territory while still finding three real doors: AI entering legal judgment, bundling as market pressure, and the 150-country compliance claim under practitioner scrutiny. Its best line, "Can software actually keep up with labor law in 150 countries? Deel says its AI now does," is skeptical without becoming reckless. B has a sharp opener, "with no accuracy numbers," but then steps on a landmine with "Deel is giving away the compliance layer it used to sell" — a confident claim the update does not support.
gaps_in_A: "Deel bundles its AI compliance tool free" slightly overstates "included for existing customers"; it catches itself in the proof section, but the headline should not outrun the fact pattern.
"a $12B company shipping an AI that makes that call" is a little too strong because the update says the tool flags risks, not that it decides classification.
"tracks all 150 in real time" adds "real time," which is not in the update. "As a company hires" is enough.
gaps_in_B: "Deel is giving away the compliance layer it used to sell" invents prior pricing. The update says the new AI tool is included for existing customers, not that Deel previously sold this layer separately.
"The prevailing belief in the category is that AI can now absorb compliance work" is an unsupported market premise. Do not manufacture the straw man just to make the contrarian angle punchier.
"competitor pricing responses land within weeks" is fake certainty. No competitor response is in the facts.

The next step, "newsjack-detector," is off. This is already launch-timed; the immediate move is proof collection and journalist-fit-check, especially accuracy data, liability posture, and lawsuit handling.
